claims.text: Oxide-growth kinetics govern whether a protective scale remains stable on CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
Lattice-mismatch stress at the oxide/metal interface governs whether the scale cracks or spalls.
Al-containing alloys form a protective Al2O3 scale that grows more slowly than chromium oxide scales.
The slow growth of Al2O3 is caused by lower ionic diffusivity.
Al2O3 has a closer lattice match to CrFeCoNiAl than the oxides formed on the Mn- and Si-containing alloys.
A closer oxide/alloy lattice match lowers interfacial strain and stress in CrFeCoNiAl.
High-temperature oxidation of the Mn-containing alloy produces multiple Mn-, Cr-, and Fe-bearing spinel oxide phases.
CrFeCoNiSi develops a multilayered, multiphase mixed-oxide scale.
Mixed oxide scales on the Mn- and Si-containing alloys have larger lattice misfits than alumina on CrFeCoNiAl.
The larger lattice misfits generate stresses that exceed scale adhesion limits and cause cracking or spallation.
Under identical exposures above 900 °C, CrFeCoNiAl will retain a more uniform, coherent, slowly thickening, and adherent oxide scale than CrFeCoNiMn and CrFeCoNiSi.
CrFeCoNiMn will exhibit measurable scale cracking or spallation because of higher interfacial stress.
CrFeCoNiSi will exhibit measurable scale cracking or spallation because of higher interfacial stress.
Related high-temperature oxidation work identifies alumina as a protective, slowly growing, chemically stable scale.
CrFeCoNiAl, CrFeCoNiMn, and CrFeCoNiSi samples will be compared under identical heating rates, atmosphere, oxygen partial pressure, and exposure duration above 900 °C.
The proposed service boundary is an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere above 900 °C for exposures lasting tens to hundreds of hours.
Comparable interfacial stresses and scale coherence across all three compositions would falsify the proposed stress-based explanation.
